items.title: [node-forge] Forge: Ed25519 signature verification accepts small-order public keys
items.summary: Summaryed25519.verify() does not reject public keys of small order, such as the identity point. Under such a key, a signature with S = 0 and a small-order R verifies for many messages, or for every message with the identity key, without any private key. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.Detailscrypto_sign_open() in lib/ed25519.js decodes the public key A with unpackneg(), which only checks that the point is on the curve, and then checks R == [S]B - [k]A with k = SHA-512(R || A || M). Nothing rejects public keys of small order: the identity point, the other 7 points of order 2, 4 or 8, and their non-canonical encodings with y >= p.With S = 0, the check becomes R == [k](-A). For a small-order A, [k](-A) is one of at most 8 small-order points, so an attacker can make a valid signature by trying the small-order values of R. For the identity key (01 00 … 00), R = identity and S = 0 verifies for every message. For the other small-order keys, a given message can be forged with high probability. No private key is involved. The S < L check added for CVE-2026-33895 (GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw) doesn't apply, because S = 0 is canonical.Keys produced by Ed25519 key generation (ed25519.generateKeyPair() or any RFC 8032 implementation) are never small-order, so signatures under them cannot be forged this way. Applications are affected when they verify signatures against a public key an attacker can choose (for example a key included with the signed data, a self-registered key, or a key in an attacker-controlled document) and rely on the signature being bound to the message: proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation or deduplication.RFC 8032 doesn't require rejecting small-order public keys, and implementations differ. libsodium rejects them, and Node.js crypto.verify() (OpenSSL) rejects these signatures.The fix rejects a public key A when [8]A is the identity point. This covers all small-order points and their non-canonical encodings.PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.3. ed25519.verify() returns false for small-order public keys.WorkaroundsBefore calling ed25519.verify() with a public key from untrusted input, reject keys whose 32-byte encoding is one of the small-order points (the identity 01 00 … 00 and the other encodings that libsodium blocks), or only verify against keys you generated or have otherwise validated.ResourcesRFC 8032, Section 5.1.7 (Ed25519 verification): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032#section-5.1.7GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw / CVE-2026-33895 (a different Ed25519 verification issue, fixed in 1.4.0): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rwSeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by @analisaperlengkapan.Proof of conceptIdentity public key A = 01 00 … 00 (32 bytes) and signature R = 01 00 … 00, S = 00 … 00 (64 bytes):forge.ed25519.verify({message: 'admin=true', encoding: 'utf8',  signature: SIG, publicKey: IDENTITY});// <= 1.4.2: true for any message; node:crypto.verify(): false// 1.4.3: falseOther small-order public keys (orders 2, 4 and 8, and non-canonical encodings) give forgeries for many messages with S = 0 and a small-order R.Regression tests are in tests/unit/ed25519.js, and the reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-6889-vf6x-f3g5.js.ImpactApplications that verify Ed25519 signatures with node-forge against a public key that an attacker can choose are affected. An attacker can provide a small-order public key and then produce signatures that verify for many or all messages without a private key, defeating checks that rely on a signature being bound to its message under that key (proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation, deduplication). Signatures under keys from honest key generation cannot be forged, and applications that only verify against their own or otherwise trusted keys are not affected.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-6889-vf6x-f3g5https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1169https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/1b77e6f20082d7484479303d0252d5f427651295https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6889-vf6x-f3g5

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: TLS client crash on an unsupported ServerHello compression method
items.summary: SummaryA forge.tls client accepts any compression method in the ServerHello, although it only offers no compression. An unknown method makes connection.process() throw an uncaught Error when the client handles ServerHelloDone, before the server is authenticated. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.DetailsThe client's ClientHello offers only the null compression method. tls.parseHelloMessage() in lib/tls.js stores the ServerHello's compression_method for the client without checking it (the code has a TODO: handle compression methods). When the client handles ServerHelloDone it calls tls.createConnectionState(), which throws Error('Unsupported compression algorithm.') for any method other than null (0) and deflate (1). The exception propagates out of connection.process().The ServerHello isn't authenticated until the server's Finished message, so an on-path attacker can change the compression byte of a genuine ServerHello; the certificate chain still verifies. Applications that pass socket data to process() without catching exceptions terminate. This includes forge.tls.wrapSocket, which calls process() from its socket data handler, and forge.http, which uses it. A deflate (1) method, also never offered, makes the handshake fail later with an error instead of a crash.Servers are not affected: a server always selects no compression.The fix fails the handshake with an illegal_parameter alert, through the connection's error callback, when the ServerHello selects any compression method other than null.PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.3.WorkaroundsCatch exceptions thrown by connection.process() and close the socket.ResourcesRFC 5246, section 7.4.1.3 (Server Hello): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.4.1.3Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client crash during the handshake, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22hSeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by @alienkeric.Proof of conceptA server (or on-path attacker) sends a ServerHello with compression_method 0xff, followed by a valid Certificate and ServerHelloDone:client.handshake();client.process(serverHello + certificate + serverHelloDone);// <= 1.4.2: throws Error: Unsupported compression algorithm.// 1.4.3: error callback with "Unsupported compression method."The reporter's PoC (a CA-issued server certificate and the default verify callback) is in tests/pocs/ghsa-w4xr-hqv8-ch44.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.ImpactApplications that use forge.tls as a client (directly, through forge.tls.wrapSocket, or through forge.http) and pass data from a network socket to connection.process() are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make process() throw before the server is authenticated; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on forge.tls are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-w4xr-hqv8-ch44https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1169https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/1d9816d333c23c523ef2bd8b24282c87db2654efhttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-w4xr-hqv8-ch44

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: ReDoS in forge.http response header and cookie trimming
items.summary:
forge.http trims response header and Set-Cookie values with the regular expression /\s*$/, which takes quadratic time on a long run of whitespace followed by another character. A server or on-path attacker can block a forge.http client for minutes with one large response header. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.Details_trimString() in lib/http.js removes trailing whitespace with str.replace(/\s*$/, ''). On a string of n whitespace characters followed by a non-whitespace character, the regular expression engine tries a match at each of the n positions and scans the rest of the run each time, so the work is O(n^2). forge.http calls _trimString() on every response header value read by response.readHeader(), and again on cookie names and values in response.getCookies(). There is no limit on header size.With Node.js 24, an 80 KB header value takes about 4 seconds to parse, and 1 MB about 10 minutes, during which the event loop (or browser tab) is blocked.forge.http is not loaded by require('node-forge'). It is part of the forge.all bundle and needs a socket pool provided by the application (historically Flash sockets via forge.xhr), so few applications use it.The fix trims trailing whitespace with a loop, as lib/pem.js has done since 1.4.1. The trimmed result is unchanged.PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.3.WorkaroundsLimit the size of HTTP response headers before passing them to forge.http, for example in the socket pool's data handler.ResourcesRelated: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x (ReDoS in PEM decoding, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-7wch-p9px-956xSeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by @manus-pi.Proof of conceptvar response = forge.http.createResponse();var ws = new Array(40001).join('	 ');response.readHeader(forge.util.createBuffer(  'HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-A: a' + ws + 'X

'));// <= 1.4.2: about 4 seconds (quadratic in the whitespace length)// 1.4.3: about 1 msRegression tests are in tests/security/ghsa-6cv4-p8m7-4r25.js.ImpactApplications that use forge.http to talk to servers they don't control are affected. The server, or an on-path attacker, can send a response header that blocks the client's event loop for minutes, denying service to everything else in the process. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-6cv4-p8m7-4r25https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1169https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/326a4d0903ee46358bc849a5c3fd96d9c21489bdhttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6cv4-p8m7-4r25

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: TLS client crash on a handshake record received without a session
items.summary: SummaryA forge.tls client throws an uncaught TypeError from connection.process() when it receives a ServerHello while it has no session: after a close_notify alert or a call to close(), or before handshake() is called. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.Detailstls.handleHandshake() in lib/tls.js updates the handshake digests with c.session.md5.update(bytes) before it calls the message handler. A client creates its session in handshake(), and c.reset() sets it to null when the connection is closed. Closing doesn't set the fail flag, and the client goes back to expecting a ServerHello, so a Handshake record received afterwards still reaches handleHandshake(), which throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5').This happens:after the server sends a close_notify alert (at any alert level);after the application calls close();before the application calls handshake().The exception propagates out of connection.process(). Applications that pass socket data to process() from a data event handler without catching exceptions, as in the README example, terminate. After a reset the connection uses no encryption, so an on-path attacker can inject the records even when the real server is honest.Servers are not affected: a server creates its session when it receives a ClientHello.The fix handles these records like other unexpected records on a closed client: they are ignored.PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.3.WorkaroundsCatch exceptions thrown by connection.process() and close the socket, or stop passing socket data to process() once the closed callback has been called and until handshake() is called again.ResourcesRFC 5246, section 7.2.1 (Closure Alerts): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.2.1Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client TypeError, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22hSeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by @manus-use.Proof of conceptvar c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...});c.handshake();// warning close_notify alert, then an empty ServerHello, in separate// process() callsc.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('15030100020100'));c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('160301000402000000'));// <= 1.4.2: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')// 1.4.3: the record is ignoredThe reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-j8rw-jp99-435v.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.ImpactApplications that use forge.tls as a client and pass data from a network socket to connection.process() are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make process() throw; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on forge.tls are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-j8rw-jp99-435vhttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1169https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/2cfaeb516cb3d4aff1c0569d39394df41c5cb17chttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j8rw-jp99-435v

items.title: [fast-xml-parser] fast-xml-parser: Quadratic CPU consumption scanning unterminated stop-node tags
items.summary: SummaryWith the non-default stopNodes option, a stop node's body with many "<a " fragments and no closing ">" anywhere after makes readStopNodeData() rescan the entire remaining input from every "<". The failed lookahead is neither cached nor bounded, so n fragments cost O(n²) before the parser throws. Availability-only (CPU exhaustion), needs the non-default stopNodes option — not benchmarked yet, see Proof of Concept.DetailsCWE-407 — Inefficient Algorithmic ComplexityCodeOrderedObjParser.js:520 — parseXml() calls readStopNodeData() after a matching stop node opensOrderedObjParser.js:810 — calls readTagExp() for every non-special <OrderedObjParser.js:688-722 — tagExpWithClosingIndex() scans to end-of-input and returns undefined when no > existsOrderedObjParser.js:812-818 — on failure, i isn't advanced, so the next < repeats the same full scanOrderedObjParser.js:423 — the main parse loop throws immediately on the same failure; only the stop-node path retriesRoot cause: a failed closing-> lookahead is neither cached nor bounded — n copies of <a  with no later > means n scans over the remaining input, O(n²) work, before it finally throws.FixThrow immediately in readStopNodeData() when readTagExp() returns undefinedOr break the loop on the first failed scanOr find the next > once and reuse/bound that resultAdd a test asserting near-linear scaling when payload size doublesProof of conceptNot benchmarked — static-analysis finding, confidence 0.5.To confirm: configure stopNodes matching a root element. Build input as '<stop>' + '<a '.repeat(n). Time parse() until it throws Unexpected end of <tag>. Start around n=10,000 and double it — quadratic should show ~4x time per doubling, linear ~2x. Control: same input with a > present, or stopNodes unset.ImpactCPU-exhaustion DoS in Node.js services parsing untrusted XML with stopNodes enabled. A ~100KB payload is estimated at ~10⁹ character operations (roughly a second or more of blocked event loop) — analytical estimate, not a benchmark. No confidentiality/integrity impact. CVSS 3.1: AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L (3.7, Low).Referenceshttps://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-474x-hrwr-fgx4https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/commit/0c3659348364959da62954b73728fb3bd05ebcb4https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/releases/tag/v5.12.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-474x-hrwr-fgx4

items.title: [mongoose] Mongoose: Discriminator key values matching inherited properties (e.g. __t: 'constructor') bypass schema casting and can poison collections
items.summary: SummaryMongoose chooses which discriminator model or schema to use by looking up the discriminator key value (__t by default) in a plain object of registered discriminators, for example Model.discriminators[doc.__t]. That value comes from user documents and query filters. Because the lookup did not check own properties, a value that names a property inherited from Object.prototype resolves to that inherited value instead of a discriminator. Examples are 'constructor', 'toString' and 'hasOwnProperty'.__t: 'constructor' resolves to the global Object function. Mongoose then calls new Object(doc), which returns the raw user object where a Mongoose document is expected.__t: 'toString' and similar names resolve to built-in functions that throw when used as a constructor or schema.The most serious effect: through bulkWrite() insertOne with skipValidation: true, the raw user object is stored as-is, without schema casting or strict filtering. After that, every query that returns the stored document throws, until the document is removed from the database.DetailsThe registries that hold discriminators are plain objects: Model.discriminators, schema.discriminators, and the embedded discriminator registries on document arrays and single nested subdocuments. Several code paths indexed them directly with a value taken from the document or filter:Code pathInputModel constructor (new Model(doc))documentModel.create(), insertMany(), bulkWrite(), bulkSave()documentsHydrating query results (find(), findOne(), etc.) and Model.hydrate()stored documentsCasting query filters, including flat paths such as 'events.__t' and $elemMatchquery filterCasting updates and array filtersupdate filter, arrayFiltersDocument array push() / create(), document array and single nested castingsubdocumentsPopulate on embedded discriminatorsstored subdocumentsgetDiscriminatorByValue() already iterated the registry's own keys safely. But most callers tried the direct lookup first and only fell back to it afterwards, so a truthy inherited value took precedence.The lookups only read inherited properties. They do not write to Object.prototype or any other shared object, and they do not change in-memory state that affects other requests. This is NOT a prototype pollution vector.Proof of conceptconst mongoose = require('mongoose');const Base = mongoose.model('Base', new mongoose.Schema({ name: String, age: Number }));Base.discriminator('Child', new mongoose.Schema({ extra: String }));// Type confusion: the "document" is the raw input objectconst doc = new Base({ name: 'x', __t: 'constructor' });console.log(doc instanceof mongoose.Document); // false// Schema bypass and persistent poison document via bulkWrite + skipValidationawait Base.bulkWrite([{  insertOne: { document: { name: 'x', age: 'not a number', notInSchema: true, __t: 'constructor' } }}], { skipValidation: true });// Stored verbatim: { age: 'not a number', notInSchema: true, __t: 'constructor', ... }await Base.find(); // throws: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'eachPath')ImpactCrashing the request. An attacker who controls the discriminator key of a document or filter can make the request fail. In most code paths that sent the value, this means a TypeError or a non-document object returned to application code. Ways in include Model.create(req.body), new Model(req.body), Model.find(req.query)-style filters, and pushing user input onto embedded discriminator arrays. The effect is limited to the request carrying the value.Schema bypass on bulkWrite({ skipValidation: true }). When an application passes untrusted documents to bulkWrite() insertOne with skipValidation: true, the raw object is stored without casting or strict filtering. Fields the schema would normally strip are persisted, such as an isAdmin that isn't in the schema. Fields with wrong types are also persisted.Persistent denial of service for queries. A stored document with such a discriminator key value makes hydration throw. Every query that returns that document fails, for all users, until the document is deleted directly in the database. Besides the bulkWrite() path above, the document can get into the collection through another application, the raw MongoDB driver, or any other writer that does not go through Mongoose casting.This issue doesn't let an attacker modify Object.prototype, built-in functions, schemas or other shared in-memory state. The schema bypass requires the application to opt in to skipValidation with untrusted input.Referenceshttps://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/security/advisories/GHSA-wr5m-5jph-8m96https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125116https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/0ecd8040d9b446f36535d79938c130c800f91766https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/18afab75bea861f625b7c5b54635c84567ec566chttps://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/390453c8ce1b36b6cfd1e63432a910da1f3d81d5https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/8cee51beead554df1f3d05645edb439c69eb2a9bhttps://github.

items.title: [mongoose] Mongoose walks into inherited properties when hydrating, setting, and merging, allowing overwrites of built-in functions (denial of service) and shared schema state
items.summary: SummaryThree Mongoose code paths copy data into objects by property name without checking whether the property is the object's own or inherited from its prototype:Loading a document from the database (init(), also used by Model.hydrate())Setting a dotted path on a document ($__set, used by new Model(obj), doc.set() and doc.$set())Merging update documents (utils.mergeClone, used by findOneAndReplace(), chained update calls and Query.prototype.merge())When a key names an inherited property, such as toString or valueOf, or a document internal such as $__schema, Mongoose writes into the shared object behind that property. The data comes from the attacker.Denial of service. For example, { "toString": { "call": 1 } } overwrites Object.prototype.toString.call. Mongoose and most other libraries rely on Object.prototype.toString.call(). After the overwrite, every later query in the process throws TypeError: _toString.call is not a function until the process restarts. This includes queries on unrelated models.Changing shared schema state. Through a subdocument with strict: false, a path such as profile.$__schema.paths.email.validators reaches the subdocument's schema, which every document shares. Setting it to [] removes the required validator for every document in the process.Mongoose already blocked __proto__, constructor and prototype, so these bugs cannot add properties to Object.prototype itself. They can still overwrite methods and properties of shared built-in functions and of Mongoose's internal objects.Details1. Loading documents: init()if (!schemaType && utils.isPOJO(value)) {  // assume nested object  if (!doc[i]) { doc[i] = {}; ... }  init(self, value, doc[i], opts, path + '.');}For a stored field named toString, doc[i] is the inherited Object.prototype.toString. It is truthy, so init() recurses into that function and copies the stored subfields onto it.This runs for every document Mongoose loads: find(), findOne(), cursors, populated documents and Model.hydrate(). It runs whatever the strict setting, and it applies to top-level and nested paths alike. lean() queries are not affected.A malicious document can get into the collection in several ways:through a model with strict: false, for example new Model(req.body).save();through another application or the raw MongoDB driver;through any update that writes arbitrary keys.2. Setting dotted paths: $__setWhen it walks a dotted path, $__set read obj[parts[i]] and descended into whatever it found. That included inherited functions, such as Object.prototype.toString on a plain object or Document.prototype.toObject on a subdocument. On subdocuments it also included non-function internals that are prototype getters, such as $__schema, schema, $__middleware and $__schemaTypeOptions. Those point at objects that every document of the model shares.Attacker-controlled input reaches this path through:A Mixed path on a default, strict schema: new Model({ "mixed.toString.call": 1 }), or doc.set({ "mixed.toString.call": 1 }). Nothing needs to be saved.Any root path on a schema with strict: false: for example doc.set('toString.call', 1).A subdocument with strict: false, when the application passes a user-controlled path to doc.set(path, value): for example doc.set('profile.$__schema.paths.email.validators', []).3. Merging updates: utils.mergeCloneif (typeof to[key] === 'undefined') {  to[key] = clone(fromObj[key]);} else if (isObject(val)) {  mergeClone(to[key], val);   // to[key] may be an inherited built-in}to[key] was read without an own-property check, so a key such as toString recursed into Object.prototype.toString. This affects:Model.findOneAndReplace(filter, replacement). It always merges the replacement into the query's update, so a single call with an untrusted replacement is enough.Update calls chained onto a query that already has an update. For example Model.updateOne(filter, { $set: {...} }).updateOne({}, untrustedUpdate), the same pattern with findOneAndUpdate(), or middleware that calls this.updateOne(...).Query.prototype.merge() with a source query whose update came from untrusted input.Proof of conceptconst mongoose = require('mongoose');const { Schema } = mongoose;// 2. Setting dotted paths: a Mixed path on a default strict schema, nothing savedconst Item = mongoose.model('Item', new Schema({ name: String, meta: {} }));new Item(JSON.parse('{"meta.toString.call": 1}'));  // e.g. new Item(req.body)console.log(typeof Object.prototype.toString.call); // 'number'// From here on, every query in the process fails:// TypeError: _toString.call is not a function// 1. Loading documents: a stored field named after an Object.prototype methodconst Loose = mongoose.model('Loose', new Schema({ name: String }, { strict: false }));await new Loose(JSON.parse('{"name":"evil","toString":{"call":1}}')).save();await Loose.findOne({ name: 'evil' });              // any later read of this documentawait OtherModel.findOne();                         // TypeError: _toString.call is n

items.title: [mongoose] Mongoose: Prototype pollution via Schema.prototype.virtual()
items.summary: SummaryPrototype pollution via Schema.prototype.virtual() — the 2022 fix for CVE-2022-2564 / CVE-2022-24304 protected Schema.path()/add() but never virtual(), so the same class of bug is still exploitable in all maintained release lines.DetailsIn lib/schema.js, Schema.prototype.virtual() (defined at line 2643) builds the virtual path via:virtuals[name] = parts.reduce(function(mem, part, i) {mem[part] || (mem[part] = (i === parts.length - 1)? new VirtualType(options, name): {});return mem[part];}, this.tree); // lines 2755-2759Unlike path()/add(), virtual() never received the specialProperties check added for CVE-2022-2564/CVE-2022-24304 (lib/schema.js lines 806, 1308, 1331).A path containing __proto__/constructor/prototype segments resolves through the prototype chain and writes onto Object.prototype / Function.prototype.Proof of conceptconst mongoose = require('mongoose');const schema = new mongoose.Schema({});schema.virtual('__proto__.polluted');console.log(({}).polluted); // VirtualType instanceconsole.log(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted')); // trueconsole.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Object.prototype, 'polluted').enumerable); // trueschema.virtual('constructor.prototype.opol');console.log(({}).opol); // trueschema.virtual('hasOwnProperty.__proto__.fpol');console.log((function(){}).fpol); // Function.prototype pollutedImpactAttacker-influenced schema field names (dynamic schemas, CMS form builders, schema-as-code) allow pollution of Object.prototype (own, enumerable keys visible on every object — e.g. ({}).isAdmin checks can be spoofed) and Function.prototype (a known gadget primitive in server-side JS).Referenceshttps://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/security/advisories/GHSA-6972-9mcm-vhwjhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125118https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/318f7e09dd363a1dfddb8180878488dccd2796d1https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/74df7769b5a8d89c4413b764029911ee915ea467https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/7a2a6567abbb72c0430c8cc5b7942141844fecffhttps://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/fb467e6d33174293dc0360649f20ce68d99117a9https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/6.13.12https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/7.8.13https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/8.24.7https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/9.11.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6972-9mcm-vhwj

items.title: [mongoose] Mongoose: Connection-level sanitizeFilter not applied
items.summary: SummarysanitizeFilter exists to stop query selector injection: it wraps operator objects such as { $ne: null } in filter values in $eq, so they are matched literally. Set on a connection with mongoose.connect() or createConnection(uri, { sanitizeFilter: true }), the connection reports it as enabled but queries never apply it. An application that relies on the connection-level option and passes an attacker-controlled object into a filter therefore remains open to selector injection, and a password value of { $ne: null } returns the account record without the password.DetailsNativeConnection#createClient() at lib/drivers/node-mongodb-native/connection.js:270-272 moves options.sanitizeFilter into Connection.config and deletes the original option. Query#_castConditions() at lib/query.js:2413-2423 checks Connection.options, the global options, and the per-query options, but never Connection.config. The defense therefore does not run even though Connection#get('sanitizeFilter') returns true. This storage was introduced in Mongoose 6.0.0 and the same mismatch is present in 9.11.2.Proof of conceptimport mongoose from 'mongoose'const conn = await mongoose.createConnection('<MONGODB_URI>', { sanitizeFilter: true }).asPromise()const User = conn.model('User', new mongoose.Schema({  username: String,  password: String,  marker: String}))await User.create({  username: 'victim',  password: 'correct-password',  marker: 'PROTECTED_RECORD'})const filter = { username: 'victim', password: { $ne: null } }console.log(conn.get('sanitizeFilter'))console.log((await User.findOne(filter).lean()).marker)A control query with a literal wrong password returned no document in the same run, confirming the filter is otherwise enforced.ImpactConnection-level sanitizeFilter option is not respected. Any user that relies on connection-level config and sanitizeFilter to defend against query selector injection is affected. Users that set sanitizeFilter globally using mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter') or on specific queries using Model.find().sanitizeFilter() are not affected.Referenceshttps://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/security/advisories/GHSA-gg4r-jv3p-qx3chttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125119https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/4bb659478be2f30655a7bdd78bc251bdf111cd29https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/4f4f9a79f860786a54133bee2c9af967ec691491https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/83eda6af1489e9ef60bb8eee8cf9ee005771b9d5https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/commit/b8970c25998c23fbccd17f76c0398b902ff4911dhttps://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/6.13.12https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/7.8.13https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/8.24.7https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/releases/tag/9.11.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gg4r-jv3p-qx3c
